messages.content: Write a post about what a software company learned from a year of remote work. Around 250 words.

**Twelve months with no office: what actually shifted**

We gave up the office in March. It wasn't a stand on the future of work. The lease ran out and nobody felt like signing another one.

A year on, here's what survived and what fell over.

Writing things down asynchronously turned out to be the whole job. Our design docs used to be paperwork nobody opened. They became the place decisions actually got made, because there was no hallway left to make them in. The docs got longer. Review threads slowed down and got better. One argument about architecture ran nine days in a comment thread and landed somewhere better than any whiteboard session I've stood at.

Onboarding fell apart. New engineers used to pick up context by overhearing it. From home they picked up nothing, and we missed it entirely until two people resigned in month five, both saying some version of "I never knew whether I was doing okay." Now everyone gets a named buddy, three scheduled check-ins in the first month, and we write down what used to just float around.

Meetings shrank, then grew back. We finished the year booking roughly the same hours we started with. That's a failure of discipline, not a failure of remote work, and we still haven't fixed it.

The surprise: seniority stopped predicting influence. The clear writers moved the company. A few genuinely good engineers who had been coasting on being convincing in a room went quiet.

We're not going back. We did stop pretending the office was doing nothing.

*(Composite account. Details are illustrative, not from a specific company.)*

output:
**A year without an office: what held and what broke**

We let the office go in March. There was no manifesto behind it. The lease expired, and none of us wanted to put a name on a new one.

Twelve months later, some of it worked and some of it didn't.

Written asynchronous work turned into the actual job. Design docs used to be filing — something you produced and nobody read. They became where decisions got made, since the hallway that used to host them was gone. Docs ran longer. Review threads got slower and sharper. One architecture disagreement stretched across nine days of comments and ended up somewhere better than any whiteboard I've stood in front of.

Onboarding broke badly. New hires had always absorbed context by overhearing it. At home they absorbed none, and we didn't notice until two people quit in month five, both saying roughly "I had no idea if I was doing fine." Now every new engineer gets a named buddy, three booked check-ins in month one, and we write down what used to drift through the air.

Meetings dropped, then crept back up. We ended the year booking about the hours we started with. That's our discipline failing, not remote work failing, and it's still not fixed.

The thing I didn't expect: seniority stopped predicting influence. People who wrote clearly moved the company. A few real talents who had coasted on being persuasive in a room went quiet.

We're staying remote. We also stopped pretending the office had contributed nothing.

*(Composite account. Details are illustrative, not from a specific company.)*
